bridges.title: The Same Fall, Closer
bridges.text: Kings tells the destruction of Jerusalem from a distance, in a few verses. The next seven chapters are the same catastrophe told from inside the walls, by a prophet who lived through the siege.

bridges.title: Two Exiles
bridges.text: The story now steps back a century and a half. When Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC, its people were deported to Nineveh; Tobit is their story. Daniel follows the later exiles of Judah to Babylon.

bridges.title: From Persia to the Greeks
bridges.text: Nehemiah ends around 430 BC in a small Persian province. A century later Alexander the Great conquered Persia, and Judea passed to his successors: first the Ptolemies of Egypt, then, from about 200 BC, the Seleucids of Syria. In Alexandria, Jewish scholars translated the Scriptures into Greek, the Septuagint, which the early church would read. 1 Maccabees opens with Alexander and moves quickly to the crisis of 167 BC.

bridges.title: The Road to Bethlehem
bridges.text: Simon's heirs, the Hasmoneans, ruled an independent Jewish state for about eighty years. In this era the Pharisees and Sadducees took shape, synagogues spread, and the community behind the Dead Sea Scrolls withdrew to the desert. Rome's general Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC. Rome later made Herod king of Judea; he rebuilt the temple on a grand scale. Luke opens in Herod's last years.

notes.text: These six verses introduce Abram, Sarai and Lot and move the family from Ur to Haran. Note verse 30: Sarai is barren. That tension drives the whole Abraham story.
For 35 chapters Job's friends insist his suffering must be punishment for hidden sin. Job maintains his innocence and demands that God answer him. Then God does.
God's rebuke of the friends in verse 7 is a ruling on the debate you skipped: God says the friends have not spoken rightly of him, as Job has.
The people swear to the covenant, sealed in blood. Eight chapters later comes the golden calf, which is why it reads as betrayal.
Numbers picks up with this same cloud lifting to lead Israel on. The two books are one motion.
Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh may settle east of the Jordan, on one condition: their soldiers fight the whole conquest first. Remember this for Joshua 22.
The Shema, Israel's central prayer. In Luke 10:27 a lawyer quotes it to Jesus as the heart of the Law.
Optional. The covenant's blessings and curses are the scorecard behind every verdict in Kings: "he did evil in the sight of the LORD."
The eastern tribes have kept the promise of Numbers 32 and are going home. What they build on the way nearly starts a civil war.
Watch for the refrain: in those days there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what was right in their own eyes.
The last verses are a genealogy kept on purpose: Ruth the Moabite is David's great-grandmother.
Skim the measurements. The story resumes when the ark comes to the temple in chapter 8.
Slow down. From here to 2 Kings 13 run the Elijah and Elisha stories, among the best storytelling in the Old Testament. Elijah reappears beside Jesus in Luke 9.
Jerusalem is under Babylonian siege. King Zedekiah wavers between surrender and resistance; Jeremiah tells him to surrender.
Catholic Bibles place a long prayer and hymn here, sung inside the furnace. Skim it like a psalm; the story resumes at 3:91.
These two stories stand at the end of Catholic Daniel. Susanna is set in Daniel's youth.
Judith's history is deliberately scrambled (Nebuchadnezzar as king of Assyria), the ancient way of saying "once upon a time." Skim the campaign; the heroine enters in chapter 8.
This is the longer Greek Esther. The Hebrew book never names God; the Greek additions, including Mordecai's dream and the queen's prayer, bring God into the story openly.
Verses 6-23 jump ahead decades to later opposition, then the story returns to its own time.
Jonah lived in the days of the kings (2 Kings 14:25). His book closes the Old Testament story here on a question God asks about mercy.
Skim from here: rival kings bargain for the Maccabees' loyalty.
Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about his "departure"; in Greek, his exodus.
The lawyer's answer is the Shema you read in Deuteronomy 6.
Optional detour: the raising of Lazarus, the one major story of Jesus that Luke does not tell. Luke 10:38-42 has already introduced Martha and Mary.
Acts ends mid-history: Paul under house arrest in Rome, preaching openly. The story is left open.
